title: India Spent 17% More in Two Months but Used Less Than a Tenth of Its Deficit Budget. Here's How.
excerpt: Fresh government data shows India's April-May fiscal deficit at just 9.6% of its full-year target — down sharply from the alarming 21% burn rate a month earlier. The capex push is real, and so are the risks.
body:
India's government burned through just 9.6% of its full-year fiscal deficit target in the first two months of the financial year, new data released on Tuesday shows — a dramatic improvement from last year and a signal that New Delhi is front-loading infrastructure spending while keeping its books unusually tight.

The April-May deficit came in at ₹1.62 trillion ($17.11 billion), compared with just ₹131.6 billion in the same period last year, according to data from the Controller General of Accounts. The year-on-year surge looks alarming in isolation, but the context tells a different story: government spending accelerated sharply while revenues held steady, and the deficit remains well within the fiscal glide path.

The Numbers That Matter

India has set its FY27 deficit target at 4.3% of GDP, or ₹16.96 trillion. At ₹1.62 trillion through May, the government has used less than a tenth of that headroom.

The spending breakdown reveals where the money is going:

  • **Total government expenditure:** ₹8.8 trillion, up from ₹7.5 trillion a year ago — a 17% jump
  • **Capital expenditure** (roads, railways, airports): ₹2.5 trillion, up from ₹2.2 trillion — a 14% increase
  • **Net tax receipts:** ₹3.5 trillion, flat compared to the same period last year
  • **Non-tax revenue:** ₹3.5 trillion, marginally down from ₹3.6 trillion

The flat tax take is notable. The government's income tax cuts from last year's budget, which removed the tax burden from millions of middle-class earners, are showing up in the revenue numbers. But the hit is being offset by front-loaded spending — particularly on infrastructure — that is designed to crowd in private investment and sustain India's growth trajectory.

> "The government's income tax cuts from last year's budget, which removed the tax burden from millions of middle-class earners, are showing up in the revenue numbers."

Why This Matters Beyond the Spreadsheet

For the uninitiated, fiscal deficit data sounds like the driest corner of economics. But for NRIs and the global investor community watching India, this data point is a temperature check on something much bigger: can India keep spending on growth without blowing up its balance sheet?

The early signal is yes. After narrowing the deficit from 9.2% of GDP in the pandemic year (FY21) to 4.4% in FY26, India is continuing to consolidate even as it raises spending. That fiscal discipline is a key reason foreign investors just poured a record $3 billion into Indian government bonds in June — the highest monthly inflow ever — following New Delhi's decision to scrap capital gains and withholding taxes on bond income.

![New Delhi — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fe/Forecourt%2C_Rashtrapati_Bhavan_-_1.jpg/3840px-Forecourt%2C_Rashtrapati_Bhavan_-_1.jpg)

"The reforms are bearing fruit, with inflows picking up," said Lavanya Venkateswaran, executive director and senior India economist at OCBC Bank.

Goldman Sachs has raised its 2026 growth forecast for India by 30 basis points and now expects a balance of payments surplus of 0.7% of GDP — a turnaround from the deficit the country ran last year.

The Risks Ahead

The early discipline doesn't mean the year is settled. Several headwinds loom:

Oil prices remain volatile. The Iran war pushed crude above $120 earlier this quarter before the interim ceasefire brought it down to around $73. If the Doha talks falter and Hormuz shipping stays constrained, fuel subsidy costs could balloon. The government already cut excise duties to shield consumers — a fiscal cost it hasn't fully absorbed.

The monsoon is running 42% below normal. Poor rainfall threatens kharif sowing, which could push food prices higher and force the government to expand food subsidies. In FY26, food subsidy spending rose nearly 50% year-on-year in the first month alone.

Tax collections need to accelerate. Net tax receipts were flat in April-May despite a growing economy, reflecting the drag from last year's income tax reforms. The government is betting on GST buoyancy and corporate tax growth to close the gap, but both depend on domestic demand holding up.

DBS economist Radhika Rao noted that "the need to accommodate higher subsidies and lower revenue growth is likely to result in a modestly wider fiscal deficit in FY27" — though still within striking distance of the 4.3% target if oil stays below $80.

What It Means for NRIs

For diaspora investors, India's fiscal trajectory is directly linked to bond yields, rupee stability, and the broader investment climate. The record bond inflows and the rupee's first quarterly gain in five quarters are not unrelated to the fiscal numbers — they're downstream of them.

India's capex push — the ₹2.5 trillion spent on infrastructure in just two months — is building the roads, ports, and railways that underpin the manufacturing and logistics story global investors are buying into. Whether that momentum holds through the monsoon and oil-price uncertainty will determine if India ends FY27 as a fiscal success story or with another mid-year scramble.

*Sources: Reuters, Controller General of Accounts (India), Goldman Sachs Research, DBS Research, OCBC Bank*
